en: Indeed, there exists no such thing as "emptiness" other than knowledge itself; for it is held that the nature of discernment is its non-separation from that which is discerned. // 1 //

For consciousness is indeed empty of duality; otherwise, it would follow that it is not so, because for one who has ceased [from] the non-existence of duality, there would be the consequence of its having the nature of duality. // 2 //
The Blessed One himself is said to have the nature of that very suchness which has been heard;
he is the non-receptacle for conceptual constructions such as the existence of the object of cognition and the cognizer. (3)
Mind-only is without appearance; such is the dwelling, and likewise the stage of the Buddhas.
This indeed has been spoken by the Buddhas, they speak it, and they cause it to be spoken. // 4 //
For the seven stages are the mind; the eighth stage here is without appearance.
Two stages are the dwelling herein; the remaining stage is of my own nature. // 5 //
The seven stages are taught by the Buddhas for those who have attained mastery over the mind;
on the seventh stage, the corruption of body, speech, and mind no longer functions.

On the eighth [day], even his dreams arise as unpleasant; his very basis of existence is such. Homage to the Buddha of inconceivable power, whose intellect is unattached, by whom the Dharma—inexpressible by words—was taught out of compassion.
2. Not arisen by way of intrinsic nature, they are not extinguished in reality;
like space, so are the Buddhas and sentient beings, possessing a single characteristic. // 9 //
3. Neither this shore nor the far shore have arisen by way of intrinsic nature; they are dependently originated.
Indeed, those conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), which are the domain of the wisdom of the Omniscient One, are empty. // 10 //
4. All phenomena are considered to be like reflections by their very nature;
they are pure, of the nature of peace, non-dual, and equal to suchness. // 11 //
5. Although there is no self, ordinary people imagine the nature of a self;
likewise, they perceive pleasure, pain, and supernormal knowledges—all of these [exist] only in reality. // 12 //
6. That which is the saṃsāra of the six destinies, as well as heaven with its supreme bliss, the great suffering in hell, and even old age and disease for those who strive [for liberation]. // 13 //
7. Having formed an unreal conceptualization, they are cooked in the hells and other realms;
they are burned by their own fault alone, just as bamboos are consumed by fire. 14.
Just as an illusion, so do sentient beings enjoy sense objects.
They go toward a state consisting of illusion, which has the nature of dependent origination. // 15 //
9. Just as a painter, having himself painted an extremely terrifying form of a yakṣa, becomes afraid of it, so too does the ignorant person [fear] within saṃsāra.
10. Just as some fool, having himself made mud, falls into it, so too are sentient beings submerged in the mud of unreal conceptualization, from which they are difficult to extricate. // 17 //
11. Seeing existence as non-existence, one experiences painful sensation;
likewise, the objects of the senses, though unreal, afflict one with the poison of doubt. 18.
And seeing those very beings who are without refuge, the Buddhas, the benefactors whose minds are steadfast in compassion, enjoin them toward perfect enlightenment. // 19 //

13. Having also accumulated the necessary provisions and attained unsurpassed gnosis, they will be liberated from the web of conceptual construction and become Buddhas, the kinsmen of the world. // 20 //
14. Since [all things] are unborn and unarisen according to those who correctly perceive the welfare of sentient beings, they see the world as empty, devoid of beginning, middle, and end. // 21 //
15. By that [wisdom], they perceive both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, yet not as belonging to a self;
it is unstained, changeless, and luminous from beginning to middle to end. // 22 //
16. One who has awakened does not see the objects experienced in a dream;
likewise, one awakened from the sleep of delusion does not see cyclic existence at all. // 23 //
17. When a magician, having conjured an illusion, withdraws it, then nothing at all exists; for that is the true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena. // 24 //
18. All this is mind-only, arisen like a magician's illusion; from that comes virtuous and non-virtuous karma, and from that comes virtuous and non-virtuous birth. // 25 //
19. People, though not themselves born [by an external cause], imagine the world as having arisen;
for this "arising" is a conceptual construction, and no external object exists. // 26 //
20. Fools, shrouded by the darkness of delusion, wander in this ocean of existence, perceiving as permanent, self, and blissful those things that lack intrinsic nature. // 27 //
Who indeed, without embarking upon the Mahāyāna, will cross to the further shore of this great ocean of saṃsāra, which is filled with the waters of conceptual construction? (28)
The *Mahāyānaviṃśikā* is the work of the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna.
